title: NIEO, WTO and the Voice of the South

cards.h: The long fight for a fairer economic order
cards.b:
Since the 1960s the developing world (the 'South') has argued that the global economic system favours the rich 'North'. In the 1970s it demanded a New International Economic Order (NIEO). Today the same fight continues in the WTO, in climate finance and in debt talks.

India has been at the centre of this story: a leader of the G77 and NAM, a strong voice in the Uruguay and Doha rounds, and, since 2023, the host of the Voice of the Global South summits.

The examiner wants the history (NIEO, UNCTAD), the theory (dependency, unequal exchange), the WTO issues (agriculture, TRIPS, subsidies) and recent events (MC12, MC13, MC14).

The G77 began in 1964 with 77 developing states at the first UNCTAD (United Nations Conference on Trade and Development), led by Raúl Prebisch. It now has over 130 members, and India is a core member.

The shock of the 1973 oil embargo showed that raw-material producers could use their leverage. At the Algiers NAM summit (1973) the South called for a new order.

The sixth special session of the UN General Assembly (April–May 1974) adopted the Declaration and Programme of Action on the Establishment of a New International Economic Order (Resolutions 3201 and 3202 (S-VI)). In December 1974 came the Charter of Economic Rights and Duties of States (Resolution 3281).

  • Permanent sovereignty over natural resources, including the right to nationalise.
  • Fair and stable commodity prices, linked to prices of manufactured imports.
  • Preferential trade access (GSP) and no reciprocity from poor countries.
  • Technology transfer and regulation of multinational firms.
  • Debt relief and more aid (the 0.7% of GNP target).
  • More voice in the IMF and World Bank.

Prebisch-Singer thesis (1950)

Raúl Prebisch and Hans Singer argued that the prices of primary goods fall relative to manufactures over time. Poor exporters lose out. Policy: industrialise by import substitution.

Dependency theory

André Gunder Frank (Capitalism and Underdevelopment in Latin America, 1967) and Samir Amin (Unequal Development, 1973) said that the periphery is kept poor by the core.

World-systems theory

Immanuel Wallerstein, The Modern World-System (1974): core, semi-periphery and periphery.

Stephen Krasner, Structural Conflict (1985)

The Third World pushed for authoritative, rule-based allocation against the market-based liberal order. He sees the NIEO as an attempt at "regime change" in global economic rules.

• Northern resistance: the US under Reagan and Britain under Thatcher backed free markets. The 1981 Cancun summit produced little.
  • Debt crisis (1982): Mexico's default began a decade of IMF structural adjustment: the Washington Consensus.
  • Divided South: oil-rich states, East Asian exporters (the 'tigers') and the poorest had different interests. OPEC's price hikes hurt non-oil poor states.
  • Rise of the WTO (1995) and rules the South had little say in.

The Brandt Report (North-South: A Programme for Survival, 1980) and the South Commission (The Challenge to the South, 1990, chaired by Julius Nyerere) kept the ideas alive.

India itself moved from import substitution to liberalisation (1991). It argued for the South in principle but joined the open system in practice.

cards.h: India in GATT and the WTO
cards.b:
• India was a founding member of GATT (1947/48) and of the WTO (1995).
  • Uruguay Round (1986–94): India opposed TRIPS and services, then accepted the package. It won the principle of special and differential treatment (S&DT).
  • Doha Round (launched 2001): called a 'development round'. India and Brazil led the G20 coalition (Cancun 2003) against farm subsidies in the rich world, and the G33 for special products and a Special Safeguard Mechanism (SSM) for farmers. Talks stalled.
  • Public stockholding (PSH): India's minimum support prices and food purchases breach WTO caps on subsidy. At Bali (2013) a 'peace clause' protects India until a permanent solution is found.
  • Dispute settlement: the Appellate Body has not worked since December 2019 because the US blocks appointments.

• MC12, Geneva (June 2022): a limited TRIPS waiver on Covid vaccines (India and South Africa had pushed for broader), a first Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies (curbing harmful subsidies), and an e-commerce moratorium extension.
  • MC13, Abu Dhabi (Feb–Mar 2024): the e-commerce moratorium was extended to MC14. No permanent PSH solution.
  • MC14, Yaoundé, Cameroon (March 2026): ended without a major deal. There was no consensus to extend the e-commerce customs-duty moratorium, so it lapsed for the first time since 1998. India and African states again asked for a permanent PSH solution; talks on fisheries continue.
  • Investment Facilitation for Development (IFD): a plurilateral deal that India has blocked from joining the WTO rulebook, arguing it goes against consensus.

As of 2026 the WTO is under severe strain: unilateral US tariffs, a paralysed Appellate Body and rising plurilaterals.

cards.h: Spokesperson for the South or a defender of its own interests?
cards.b:
Supporters say India protects 800 million food-subsidy beneficiaries and farmers' livelihoods, and defends policy space for development. Critics say India's position is defensive and blocks deals that could help smaller developing states, and that India's own growth makes it a different kind of actor.

India's reply: it is not a spoiler but a champion of consensus and of S&DT. The Voice of the Global South summits are one more effort to bring the South's demands to the G20 and beyond.

• WTO: defend PSH, S&DT and TRIPS flexibility; resist non-trade issues like labour and environment standards; support restoring the Appellate Body.
  • G20 2023: pushed debt restructuring, reform of multilateral development banks and climate finance; brought in the AU.
  • Voice of the Global South summits (January 2023, November 2023, August 2024) collected views from over 100 countries.
  • FTAs: India now signs bilateral trade deals (UAE, Australia, UK, EFTA, EU) as the WTO stalls.
  • UN: backs reform of the IMF and UNSC for fairer representation.

"Discuss the New International Economic Order and why it failed." (typical)
"India's role in the Doha Round and the WTO: examine." (typical)
"How is India working as a voice of the Global South?" (typical)

Structure: (1) background: UNCTAD, G77; (2) NIEO demands (1974); (3) theory: Prebisch-Singer, dependency; (4) why it faded: debt crisis, divisions; (5) India in GATT/WTO: S&DT, PSH, G20 and G33; (6) MC12–MC14; (7) Voice of the Global South; (8) assessment.
